strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: using existing slot annotations to improve task-oriented dialogue embeddings. Combining utterance, template, and cross-view contrastive losses is a practical, understandable approach.

Results across five established datasets are encouraging. In Table 2, TaDSE with MLP achieves 83.87 average accuracy versus 81.82 for DSE, the strongest reported baseline by average. The augmentation-adapted baselines provide useful evidence beyond comparisons with untouched checkpoints.

The augmentation and loss ablations support the value of template-aware training beyond synthetic utterances alone. Experiments with automatically extracted, noisy CLINC150 slots broaden the evidence beyond manually annotated templates, and the paper acknowledges several limitations.
weaknesses: Important experimental controls are unclear. Appendix C allows eight training epochs for the single-source MLP variant versus two for other models, confounding architectural and training-budget effects. Table 4's CLINC150 augmentation-only and full-model results match different augmentation levels in Table 3, so whether data are held fixed across loss ablations needs clarification. Epoch choices are also justified using test-set curves in Figure 8; model selection should demonstrably use development data.

The supervision regime needs more precise framing. Four datasets use human slot annotations, making the method annotation-assisted even though encoder training does not use intent labels. No annotation-budget experiment establishes the claimed low-cost advantage. Semantic compression additionally requires templates at inference, but the provenance of test-time slots is insufficiently explicit. Results with predicted slots across the annotated datasets would better establish practical applicability.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful checkpoint and training details. The three contrastive temperatures, optimizer configuration, pooling details, and validation splits are not specified adequately. Appendix C's 'full utterance/template training set representations' leaves the exact nearest-neighbor reference pool and its consistency across methods unclear. Equation 3 can also treat another utterance sharing the anchor's template as a negative; any collision handling should be documented. These details materially affect reproducing and interpreting the gains.

The paper provides no repeated-run variability or statistical uncertainty, limiting confidence in smaller improvements and claims of significant superiority. Evaluation covers one downstream task, one backbone, and full-reference-set nearest-neighbor classification; it does not establish performance under reduced annotation budgets or unseen domains. The newer commercial embedding comparison covers only two datasets, providing limited support for the broader state-of-the-art claim.

Semantic compression is an interesting heuristic, but its proposed diagnostic interpretation is insufficiently established. Table 5 shows small gains on SNIPS and ATIS and generally worse results on MASSIVE and CLINC150. Neither t-SNE plots nor qualitative alignment/uniformity trends establish that the optimal interpolation coefficient measures semantic well-formedness. Normalization details and simple interpolation controls are needed to distinguish semantic effects from vector contraction. Together with the experimental and reproducibility uncertainties, this leaves the paper borderline for Findings despite its promising central approach.
